summary: The developer machine has the essential runtime, MCP servers, and DocumentDB agent skills needed to start building the Python LangChain + DocumentDB sample. Key authoritative facts were verified and several cold answers were shown to be incorrect or outdated (mostly because they described Azure Cosmos DB (RU) or generic MongoDB rather than the managed Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters resource). No build-blocking gaps were found, but a few useful developer tools are missing (mongosh, bicep/terraform) and a few specification choices are left to the builder (Python minor version, AI provider/model and embedding dimension, seed data shape).
summary_points: All core build dependencies for the sample are present: python (venv), pip, Docker, node/npx, az CLI (signed in), the documentdb MCP server, the learn docs MCP server, and a comprehensive set of documentdb-* agent skills.

Several cold answers were incorrect because they described Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model / cosmos.* hostnames) or generic MongoDB 7.x features rather than the current Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters resource and its APIs; authoritative docs were found to correct each one.
No MCP server or skill required by the sample is missing: the documentdb MCP data-plane server and the documentdb-* skills are installed and available to the builder.
Missing but non-blocking developer utilities: mongosh (useful for manual checks) and IaC CLIs (bicep, terraform) — useful but not required because the run policy forbids provisioning.

Information gaps remain that the builder must pick: Python minor version to pin, embeddings/model selection and embedding dimension (if vectors used), and concrete sample document schema/seed data (small idempotent seed script is required).

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (ARM): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (commonly called a Cosmos DB account).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct ARM resource type for the managed MongoDB clusters that this sample uses is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider Microsoft.DocumentDB, resource type 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace and historical naming: older Cosmos DB examples use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the new managed MongoDB product uses the same provider but a different resource type (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in templates or CLI commands they would create/manage a Cosmos DB account (or fail), not the mongoClusters resource the sample expects; IaC and CLI commands would be wrong.
improvements: Add a short note on the Quickstart page and in the documentdb-azure-deployment skill: 'Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for DocumentDB managed MongoDB clusters; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB) for this product.'
Add a deprecation/clarification banner on pages that still show databaseAccounts for MongoDB workloads to reduce accidental reuse.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create ... This is provided by the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI command group for the managed MongoDB clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (and there is also az cosmosdb mongocluster in some docs). The functionality is exposed via the Azure CLI 'documentdb' extension/command group. You may need the documentdb extension; the az CLI can prompt to install it.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services (Cosmos DB accounts and the new DocumentDB clusters) operate in the same broad domain and the older cosmosdb CLI group historically handled Cosmos resources; docs and CLI extensions have overlapping names (az cosmosdb vs az documentdb).
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create or the wrong CLI command group could attempt to manage a Cosmos DB account rather than the mongoClusters resource or require different parameters; CLI reference commands in scripts would fail or target the wrong resource.
improvements: Make the Quickstart CLI page explicitly state the recommended CLI group (az documentdb mongocluster) and call out aliasing or the availability of az cosmosdb mongocluster to avoid confusion.
In the documentdb-mcp-setup skill, add an example of how to ensure the az 'documentdb' extension is installed and how to call az documentdb mongocluster create/show/list-connection-strings.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For managed Azure DocumentDB MongoDB clusters you should use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM. Terraform examples use the Microsoft templates/azapi or the mongo-cluster-specific module (reference docs show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoclusters usage). The azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource targets Cosmos DB databaseAccounts and is the wrong resource for mongoClusters.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn templates pages for mongoClusters

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older CosmosDB 'databaseAccounts' resource was commonly used for Mongo-compatible accounts; the new managed service uses a dedicated resource type 'mongoClusters'.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses azurerm_cosmosdb_account or Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in deployment templates, they will provision a different service (Cosmos DB) or the template will not match the expected managed mongo cluster shape; automation and docs will be incorrect.
improvements: Add a migration note on the Bicep/ARM 'databaseAccounts' doc pointing to the new 'mongoClusters' resource when the user intends to create a managed MongoDB cluster.

In the documentdb-azure-deployment skill, include canonical Bicep and Terraform snippets for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and an explicit 'do not use databaseAccounts for DocumentDB mongoClusters' guidance.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Scheme: mongodb:// (or mongodb+srv:// for SRV if supported). Host suffix: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (port typically 10255). ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters the connection string typically uses mongodb+srv:// or mongodb:// with the cluster-specific endpoint (e.g. <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or other cluster DNS suggested by list-connection-strings). The cluster provides connection strings via az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (or portal). The portal/CLI returns mongodb+srv/ mongodb+srv-style URIs and the service supports SCRAM-SHA-256; ports and options differ from classic Cosmos DB 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255' URIs. Always use the exact connection string from the cluster.

grounding_links.title: Get connection strings for a mongo cluster (az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings examples)
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (PowerShell)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) style hostnames and port (mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255). Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters expose different endpoints and may provide SRV-style endpoints and different connection options.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port (10255 + mongo.cosmos.azure.com) would cause authentication/connection failures or incorrect TLS/driver options; the app might fail to connect or connect to the wrong service.
improvements: On the Quickstart and SDK quickstart pages, explicitly show an example cluster connection string for mongoClusters (mongodb+srv://<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/...) and call out differences from Cosmos DB's old mongo endpoints.
In the documentdb-driver skill, add a 'copy connection string from portal/az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings' instruction and an example of how to parse/use that string safely.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Billing is RU-based (Request Units/sec) for Cosmos DB accounts: you can provision fixed RU/s, autoscale RU/s, or use serverless (pay per RU consumed) where available.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (managed MongoDB cluster) is billed by compute tier (vCores / M-series tiers) and storage. It is not RU/s billed — RUs are the Cosmos DB model. The DocumentDB product uses cluster tiers (M10, M20, M30, etc.), storage per shard, and optional HA/replicas; pricing docs describe compute + storage billing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Azure DocumentDB FAQ (how it relates to Cosmos DB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer corresponds to Cosmos DB's RU model. The two services (Azure DocumentDB and Cosmos DB for MongoDB RU) both relate to document DBs and share some historic naming, causing confusion.

confusion_sources.title: What is Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL? (general Cosmos overview)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU billing they may pick wrong provisioning patterns or rely on autoscale RUs; index/throughput choices and cost estimates would be wrong.
improvements: Add a bold note on Compare/Overview pages: 'Azure DocumentDB uses a compute-tier (vCore) + storage billing model — not RU/s — and is a separate product from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU).'
In the documentdb-azure-deployment skill, include an explicit costing snippet that contrasts a sample vCore-based DocumentDB cluster vs RU-based Cosmos DB for the same workload.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary authentication is via MongoDB credentials in the URI ... native Azure AD (Entra) token-based authentication is not generally available for application data plane connections.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports NativeAuth (SCRAM-SHA-256) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC / 'MONGODB-OIDC') for data-plane authentication. A cluster can be configured to allow MicrosoftEntraID; clients present an Entra-issued OIDC access token to the driver when using Microsoft Entra ID authentication. The docs show how to enable MicrosoftEntraID and that the auth mode names include 'MicrosoftEntraID' and 'NativeAuth'.
confusions.grounding_source: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

grounding_links.title: Enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication for a cluster
AuthenticationMode (KnownAuthenticationMode) docs

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API accounts historically did not have the same Entra data-plane auth modes; the cold answer reflects that history and conflates the two products.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unavailable, they may implement less secure credential management or miss simpler managed-identity flows; conversely if they assume Entra ID without enabling it on the cluster, connections will fail.
improvements: In the documentdb-security skill and quickstarts, add a worked example showing how to exchange an Entra token and connect with a MongoDB driver using MONGODB-OIDC, plus the CLI/Bicep snippet to enable MicrosoftEntraID.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access use standard MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo). For management use azure-mgmt-cosmosdb or az cli. There is no separate application-level SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: application-level code should use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python). Management/control-plane operations use the Azure control-plane SDKs or az CLI. The official quickstarts demonstrate PyMongo usage.
confusions.grounding_source: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { 'knn': { 'vectorSize': 1536, 'distance': 'cosine' } , name: 'embedding_idx'}) ... backend-specific params (method:'hnsw', m:16...).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides integrated vector indexes with kinds 'vector-ivf', 'vector-hnsw' and 'vector-diskann' (DiskANN) and creates them using the DB's createIndexes / create_index flows with 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' naming. The createIndexes JSON uses cosmosSearchOptions with parameters like 'kind', 'dimensions', 'similarity', and algorithm-specific options (m, efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, etc.). This differs from MongoDB 7's knnVector index syntax.
confusions.grounding_source: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs)

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)
Vector search examples (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described MongoDB 7.0/knnVector syntax that some databases (MongoDB) or providers use; Azure DocumentDB uses 'cosmosSearchOptions' with explicit 'vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann' kinds.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB 7.0 knnVector index examples (not from Microsoft docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using knnVector/MongoDB 7 native index syntax against DocumentDB could fail because option names differ; the index might not be created or might be created with incorrect parameters.
improvements: Add a short example on the LangChain/quickstart pages and in the documentdb-vector-search skill showing a minimal createIndexes JSON with cosmosSearchOptions for vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann and the exact field names to use in the Python/pymongo driver.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes and $text operator; hybrid (text + vector) typically done by Azure Cognitive Search or external search engine or get vector candidates then filter/rank by text.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated full-text search and vector search and supports hybrid search in a single pipeline: createSearchIndexes / integrated search indexes and use the aggregation $search stage with the 'cosmosSearch' operator. Hybrid retrieval can be done with cosmosSearch that combines lexical and vector filtering/ranking (no mandatory separate Cognitive Search pipeline).

grounding_links.title: Full-text and vector search integrated in Azure DocumentDB
Create search indexes and use $search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described common architectures that pair vector DBs with an external search engine (Azure Cognitive Search or Atlas Search). Azure DocumentDB, however, offers integrated search and vector capabilities, so an external engine is optional.
confusions.build_risk: Architecting a separate search index and ETL when DocumentDB provides integrated hybrid search increases complexity and cost and risks out-of-sync data pipelines.
improvements: Update LangChain and build-RAG guidance pages to show a canonical example of a single $search / cosmosSearch aggregation that demonstrates fusing vector + lexical filters so builders default to the integrated approach.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Varies by account: commonly advertised compatibility with MongoDB 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0 etc; not all server features supported; change streams may differ.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0 through 8.0 (compatibility tables exist per server version). The service supports most MongoDB features (99.03% operator coverage) but some administrative/server-only commands and a few operators are restricted; compatibility tables are published per version. Test queries using the compatibility reference and the migration extension.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was vague and reflected older or mixed-version support; authoritative docs list supported wire protocol versions explicitly.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming older or different protocol compatibility could lead to use of operators or client features that fail at runtime.
improvements: Add a short 'supported MongoDB versions' badge on the main DocumentDB overview and quickstarts so sample authors pick the correct driver options and feature set for their target cluster.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator; use official MongoDB docker image on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: You can run the open-source DocumentDB gateway locally (DocumentDB local Docker image) for development. The DocumentDB local gateway listens on port 10260 by default; the docs provide a docker run example and a connection string using port 10260 (TLS and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local testing).

grounding_links.title: Development loop: run DocumentDB in Docker (local gateway)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB (getting started)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed only generic MongoDB server is usable locally; Microsoft provides a DocumentDB local container/gateway specifically for development.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used a generic Mongo image they would not reproduce DocumentDB-specific behaviours (gateway options, ports, integrated vector/search features) and may miss service-specific compatibility issues.
improvements: In the documentdb-local-deployment skill, highlight the docker pull/run example and the 10260 port prominently so builders use the local gateway when appropriate.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB provides a change feed for the Cosmos APIs; MongoDB API historically did not fully support MongoDB change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams and provides a change-stream feature; multishard clusters may require enabling the change-stream feature for multishard scenarios. Docs and tutorials show usage (Model.watch(), Azure Functions triggers) and indicate you may need to enable preview features for multishard change streams in some situations.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose tutorial - Model.watch() uses change streams

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical limitations on Cosmos DB's Mongo API made some assume change streams were missing; the new DocumentDB service supports change streams with configuration considerations.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unavailable would lead to selecting a less efficient migration or real-time architecture (polling rather than event-driven).
improvements: Add a short 'change streams' usage note in the migration and quickstart docs that lists enabling steps for multishard clusters and code samples for common drivers.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane inspection and tools. The general azure MCP server covers ARM/resource management aspects but documentdb MCP provides data-plane helpers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: documentdb MCP server provides data-plane query/index/aggregation/explain tools tailored to the cluster; azure MCP covers control-plane/resource management but not the same level of data-plane inspection.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server present) and skills

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a NoSQL service called DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB... The Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API' is an API surface that implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of the Cosmos DB engine. It is not the original open-source DocumentDB project; DocumentDB was an early Microsoft service name and Cosmos DB is the successor platform.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but incomplete: the product now called Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) was previously shipped under names including 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' or 'Cosmos DB (vCore) for MongoDB' and has since been rebranded as Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) to reflect the open-source DocumentDB engine beneath it. It is distinct from the old 2014 'DocumentDB' service that became Cosmos DB, and it is not Amazon DocumentDB. The docs clarify naming and the relation to Cosmos DB and the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
FAQ: Azure DocumentDB relation to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: There have been multiple overlapping product names over time (DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore), and the new Azure DocumentDB name), producing ambiguity in memory.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the wrong product name in documentation or code examples they may cause confusion for users or pick wrong Azure services when scripting.
improvements: Add a single 'naming and lineage' section on the DocumentDB overview page that lists previous names and clarifies how Azure DocumentDB (vCore) relates to Cosmos DB and the open-source DocumentDB project, suitable for copy/paste into sample READMEs.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath the MongoDB API is the Azure Cosmos DB engine (a proprietary distributed storage and indexing system) that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect subtle differences ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For the managed DocumentDB service the underlying engine is the open-source DocumentDB engine (not MongoDB server). Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo etc.) without driver-level changes, but you must check compatibility for some admin commands and run the compatibility assessment for complex features. The difference matters for licensing and for exact unsupported admin commands; typical app-level code is unchanged.
confusions.grounding_source: Azure DocumentDB overview and compatibility docs

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
MongoDB compatibility reference

confusions.question: Which database name must the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database name sample_customer_360_08 for everything the sample creates and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: the skill_md explicitly instructs to use sample_customer_360_08 as the target database for the sample.

confusions.question: How should the sample obtain the cluster connection string at runtime?

confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: skill_md explicitly requires using DOCUMENTDB_URI from environment and not writing secrets to logs or files.

confusions.question: What collection and index will the sample create for storing customer profiles and vector embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create customers collection with vector field 'embedding' and index embedding with knnVector options {vectorSize:1536,...} plus customer_id unique index. Adapt knn/index options to exact server syntax.
confusions.grounded_answer: Create a 'customers' collection and a unique index on {customer_id:1}. For vector indexing use the service's createIndexes API with 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' and the appropriate 'kind' ('vector-hnsw', 'vector-ivf', or 'vector-diskann') plus dimensions and algorithm parameters (dimensions, similarity, m/efConstruction or numLists). The exact createIndexes JSON differs from MongoDB 7 knnVector syntax.

grounding_links.title: Create a vector index (cosmosSearchOptions examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used MongoDB-native knnVector index syntax; Azure DocumentDB requires cosmosSearchOptions with different field names and 'kind' values.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample tries to create a knnVector index via pymongo with wrong option names it will fail or create an incorrect index; searches will not return expected results.
improvements: In the sample README and in documentdb-vector-search skill, add a concrete createIndexes JSON snippet for the 'customers' collection showing cosmosSearchOptions for vector-hnsw with a sample dimensions value and algorithm args.

confusions.question: Which client libraries and pip installs should the sample use to implement the LangChain agent and DB access?
confusions.cold_answer: Install pymongo and langchain; pip install pymongo langchain openai; use MongoClient and LangChain.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use pymongo for DB access and install a LangChain integration that supports Azure DocumentDB (for example, 'langchain-azure-ai' or langchain-core plus the chosen provider). If you plan to use embeddings/LLMs, include the chosen provider package (openai or azure openai sdk). The sample should pin package versions and may prefer langchain-azure-ai or langchain-core + provider bindings; also include 'pymongo' in requirements.
confusions.grounding_source: LangChain + Azure DocumentDB integration docs and quickstarts

grounding_links.title: Use LangChain on Azure with Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer omitted the newer 'langchain-azure-ai' or provider-specific integration packages and did not insist on pinning versions or on adding the embedding/model provider dependency.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses only 'langchain' without the provider-specific or Azure integration packages, some convenience integrations (vector store connectors) may not work out-of-the-box.
improvements: Add a recommended requirements.txt template in the sample that includes 'pymongo', 'langchain-azure-ai' (or 'langchain' plus chosen provider), and the embedding/provider SDK (openai or azure-ai-openai) with pinned versions.

confusions.question: How should the agent write a computed segment label back to a customer profile document?
confusions.cold_answer: Use an update operation: db.customers.update_one({'customer_id': cid}, {'$set': {'segment': 'segment_label','segmentation_ts': datetime.utcnow()}}).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use a MongoDB update_one (pymongo) call to set the 'segment' field and a timestamp. For atomic read-modify semantics, findOneAndUpdate (find_and_modify) can be used. The documentdb MCP find_and_modify tool is available for verification.
confusions.grounding_source: pymongo and documentdb MCP update docs / Quickstart

information_gaps.title: Python minor version & dependency pins
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't pick a specific Python minor version for the sample (inventory shows Python 3.13). The builder must pick a target (3.10/3.11/3.12/3.13) and pin dependency versions in requirements.txt; I checked the prompt review and skill_md but found no pinned runtime version guidance.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and dimension
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't choose an embedding provider/model or dimension. The DocumentDB vector indexes require a matching 'dimensions' parameter; Microsoft docs list supported dimensions (DiskANN up to 16,000). The builder must decide the model and dimension (I searched vector-search docs but the sample still must pick a concrete embedding model).

information_gaps.title: Seed data shape and idempotent seed script
information_gaps.description: No concrete sample documents or seed dataset shape are provided in skills or docs; the builder needs to define 'events' and 'customers' document shapes, timestamp format, category field names and write an idempotent seed script. I looked in the local-deployment and quickstart pages but they do not supply the exact sample data needed for behavioural aggregation.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the ARM/Bicep resource type when you write any deployment templates; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for this product.
Call the cluster with the documentdb CLI group (az documentdb mongocluster ...) or the documentdb az extension; do not rely on az cosmosdb create commands for creating mongoClusters.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: When creating vector indexes, use createIndexes with 'cosmosSearchOptions' and 'kind' set to 'vector-hnsw', 'vector-ivf', or 'vector-diskann' and set dimensions/similarity/algorithm parameters per the vector-search docs; do not reuse MongoDB 7 knnVector option names.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime and pass it to MongoClient (pymongo). Do not encode credentials in code or logs; retrieve connection strings from az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or portal when needed.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh to allow interactive connectivity checks and ad-hoc explain/index checks (recommended for developer ergonomics). On many platforms: 'npm install -g mongosh' or follow the official download instructions linked from MongoDB docs.

references.title: Connect with mongosh in local quickstart (DocumentDB docs show example)

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample run (the cluster already exists and azure writes are not allowed). If you want to include or validate Bicep infra locally later, install the Bicep CLI (az bicep install). For samples, provide Bicep files but do not run them in this environment.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the live-cluster verification run; include Terraform files in the repo for users but do not execute here. If you want the ability to run IaC in this environment, install Terraform via distribution package manager.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Azure Developer CLI is convenient for full app dev+deploy flows but not necessary for a single-sample Python LangChain + DocumentDB demo that uses the live cluster.
